title: Implement Magic Dictionary
description: Brute force to optimized: direct same-length comparison with a difference counter, and a trie-DFS generalization for scale.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a MagicDictionary supporting buildDict(dictionary), which stores a list of words, and search(searchWord), which returns true if changing EXACTLY one character of searchWord results in a word present in the dictionary.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Change EXACTLY one character to match a dictionary word\"","A linear scan comparing character-by-character with a difference counter directly solves this within the given small constraints"],["\"Words can share structure\"","A trie plus DFS that permits exactly one mismatch along the walk generalizes this technique for larger inputs"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For a dictionary word to be a valid match, it must have the SAME LENGTH as searchWord, and comparing them position by position must reveal EXACTLY one differing character (not zero, since that would mean no change was made, and not more than one).

blocks.title: Analogy: Spotting a Word That Is One Typo Away
blocks.text: Picture scanning a small list of known words to see if any one of them is exactly one typo (one substituted letter) away from a given word. Same length is required, and comparing letter by letter while counting mismatches immediately reveals whether exactly one differs.

blocks.caption: Same length required; count differing positions; exactly one means a valid match

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: dictionary = ["hello", "leetcode"]

search("hello")=false (identical, zero differences, not a match). search("hhllo")=true (differs from "hello" at exactly one position). search("hell")=false (wrong length). search("leetcoded")=false (wrong length).
5. How Should We Think?

Given the small constraints (at most 100 words, each at most 100 characters, at most 100 search calls), a direct linear scan comparing searchWord against each same-length dictionary word, counting differing positions, is simple, correct, and efficient enough.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Any dictionary word with a DIFFERENT length than searchWord can immediately be skipped, since changing one character never changes a string's length.

Observation 2: For same-length words, counting the number of positions where the two strings differ tells us immediately whether exactly one substitution would suffice.

Observation 3: If that count is exactly one, searchWord is one character-substitution away from that dictionary word, a valid match.

Observation 4: If NO dictionary word achieves exactly one differing position, no valid match exists.
This leads to a straightforward same-length filter plus a differing-position counter per candidate word, matching if the count is exactly one for any word.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every dictionary word of the same length as searchWord, count differing character positions directly and check if the count equals exactly one.
Why the code is written this way

items: Comparing directly against every same-length word implements the definition clearly.
Given the small constraints, this direct approach is already efficient in practice; a trie-based DFS with one allowed mismatch generalizes this for much larger inputs.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times word length) per search.
Space: O(total dictionary characters).
Limitation: for much larger dictionaries, a trie with a DFS allowing exactly one mismatch along the walk shares common prefixes across words, avoiding a full linear scan per search.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a trie from all dictionary words. For search, perform a DFS over the trie in step with searchWord's characters, tracking how many mismatches have been used so far (0 or 1). At each step, if the current searchWord character matches a trie child, continue along that child with the SAME mismatch count. If it does not match, try continuing along a DIFFERENT child ONLY if no mismatch has been used yet (using up the one allowed substitution). Succeed if the DFS ever reaches the end of searchWord at a trie node marked end-of-word, having used EXACTLY one mismatch (not zero).
For larger inputs, a trie plus DFS tracking one allowed mismatch generalizes the same idea while sharing structure across dictionary words.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for search("hhllo") against dictionary word "hello"

blocks.text: Why This Works

Filtering to same-length words first is necessary since a single character substitution can never change a string's length. Counting differing positions directly and checking for exactly one correctly captures the "change exactly one character" requirement: zero differences means searchWord is already in the dictionary (not a valid match), and more than one difference means no single substitution suffices.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times word length) per search.
Space: O(total dictionary characters).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Implement Magic Dictionary rewards recognizing that "exactly one differing character" is simply counted directly for these constraints, with a trie-based DFS as a natural generalization for larger inputs.
Common Mistakes

items: Returning true when a dictionary word is IDENTICAL to searchWord (zero differences), which is not a valid "exactly one change" match.
Forgetting to filter by length first, potentially comparing strings of different lengths incorrectly.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "same length required, then count differing positions, exactly one needed" clarifies the exact matching condition precisely.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "change exactly one character to match a dictionary entry", think: same length filter plus a differing-position counter, or a trie DFS tracking one allowed mismatch for scale.

12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: same-length filter plus a differing-position counter (or a trie DFS with one allowed mismatch at scale).
Core Idea: exactly one differing character means a valid one-substitution match; zero or more than one does not.
Time: O(number of words times length) per search.
Most Important Observation: filtering by length first avoids meaningless comparisons.
Interview Difficulty: a straightforward design problem given its small constraints.
One line memory trick: same length, count differences, exactly one wins.
